title: The impact of the coronavirus so far: the industries that struggled or recovered
meta_description:
Temporary closures, a shift to online shopping and reduced travel meant the first wave of 
the coronavirus (COVID-19) had an enormous impact on business – but some industries fared far worse than others.

breadcrumb.text: The impact of the coronavirus so far: the industries that struggled or recovered

lede: Temporary closures, a shift to online shopping and reduced travel meant the first wave of the coronavirus (COVID-19) had an enormous impact on business – but some industries fared far worse than others.

body.text: 9 December 2020
The economic downturn resulting from coronavirus (COVID-19) restrictions has been concentrated among certain types of business.

Overall, the UK economy, measured by gross domestic product (GDP), shrank by a record 19.8% in the second quarter (April to June) of 2020, following the start of the first lockdown on 23 March. By September 2020, GDP was still down 8.2% compared with February.

Services such as hospitality – including pubs, restaurants and hotels – recorded almost no output in April and May, but industries such as information and communication, where staff could largely work from home, saw little change compared with February.

Consumer-facing services have since bounced back to some extent, but they remain significantly smaller than they were in February. At this stage, it is difficult to separate temporary losses of output, brought about by coronavirus restrictions, from longer term behavioural changes that could affect industries for years to come.

body.h4: While some industries shrank by up to 90% in April and May, others recorded marginal growth
body.text: Even within industries, different types of business have so far either struggled, recovered or – in some cases – saw trade grow in the pandemic based on what they sold and how they were able to get it to their customers.

body.h4: While some industries shrank by up to 90% in April and May, others recorded marginal growth
body.text: Here are some of the ways different types of business within the same industries fared:

body.h2: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend
body.text: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend

body.h2: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend
body.text: The enforced closure of shops selling non-essential items during the first wave of the pandemic led to a boost for online retailers.

body.h2: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend
body.text: The Office for National Statistics (ONS) October 2020 [retail sales publication](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/retailindustry/bulletins/retailsales/October2020) reported “online sales reaching higher than usual levels over the course of the pandemic”. Online purchases represented 28.5% of total sales in October compared with 20.1% in February.

body.h2: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend
body.text: The internet’s share of retail sales dipped after shops reopened in June but the proportion was increasing again in October. The extent of a structural shift in the behaviour of consumers remains to be seen.

body.h2: Online shopping grew far more than its pre-pandemic trend
body.text: While some parts of the retail industry recovered once restrictions were eased, in others, the temporary closures had effects that lasted beyond the first UK lockdown.

body.h2: Chemists traded constantly above pre-pandemic levels, while furniture store customers came back after lockdown
body.text: Chemists traded constantly above pre-pandemic levels, while furniture store customers came back after lockdown

body.h2: Chemists traded constantly above pre-pandemic levels, while furniture store customers came back after lockdown
body.text: Dispensing chemists sold consistently more since the pandemic began than they did before. As one of the essential types of shop allowed to remain open during the first lockdown, their sales rose strongly in March 2020, but they carried on growing in June even after restrictions were eased and other non-essential stores were allowed to reopen. Non-specialised food stores, which include supermarkets, also traded consistently above their pre-pandemic levels.

body.h2: Chemists traded constantly above pre-pandemic levels, while furniture store customers came back after lockdown
body.text: Retailers that relied on customers being able to visit their stores – rather than selling online – recorded a big drop after they were ordered to close their doors. However, for furniture retailers, customers returned in the summer with trade returning to pre-pandemic levels and growing further, boosted by people still spending more time at home than they used to.

body.h2: Camping saw an increase in turnover on last year while other parts of the accommodation industry saw a fall
body.text: Camping saw an increase in turnover on last year while other parts of the accommodation industry saw a fall

body.h2: Camping saw an increase in turnover on last year while other parts of the accommodation industry saw a fall
body.text: Even when restrictions in the UK were eased and people were allowed to go on their summer holidays, turnover in the accommodation industry was still down compared with a year ago.

body.h2: Camping saw an increase in turnover on last year while other parts of the accommodation industry saw a fall
body.text: That was not the case across the entire sector, with camping proving popular and even surpassing its performance last year. Some of this may be down to people deciding to holiday in the UK because of international travel restrictions and the possibility of having to quarantine on their return to the UK. Other types of accommodation, such as hotels, remained depressed suggesting that people may have believed it would be easier to socially distance on a campsite than in buildings.

body.h2: Clothing and footwear sales were still down as people socialised less
body.text: Clothing and footwear sales were still down as people socialised less

body.h2: Clothing and footwear sales were still down as people socialised less
body.text: Retail sales of clothing and footwear and leather goods fell in March and April 2020, as non-essential shops closed. Restrictions on social interactions meant people also had less of a reason to buy new clothes.

body.h2: Clothing and footwear sales were still down as people socialised less
body.text: As students prepared to return to school in September and needed new shoes, sales of footwear and leather goods picked up significantly. As with other types of clothing, however, sales in September and October 2020 were still below their February levels.

body.h2: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business
body.text: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business

body.h2: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business
body.text: Smaller firms were more likely than bigger ones to have had to temporarily close or pause trading during the pandemic, but that was not necessarily the same across all industries.

body.h2: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business
body.text: The [Business Impact of Coronavirus (COVID-19) Survey (Wave 17)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/businessservices/bulletins/coronavirusandtheeconomicimpactsontheuk/19november2020) found 17.2% of micro businesses (fewer than 10 workers) were pausing trade or temporarily closed as of late October 2020 compared with 6.1% of firms with 250 or more workers.

body.h2: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business
body.text: One area where this was noticeable was the services industry. Larger services businesses outperformed small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in terms of turnover since March 2020. According to [analysis by the Bank of England](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/bank-overground/2020/how-has-covid-19-affected-small-uk-companies), the pandemic reduced cash flows for many companies, with smaller companies "more likely than larger companies to operate in sectors that have been most affected by the shock, such as accommodation and food, arts and recreation, and construction”.

body.h2: Size didn’t matter as much as the type of business
body.text: In manufacturing, however, there did not appear to be a notable difference between SMEs and larger firms. Turnover levels for both smaller and larger firms have moved in line with each other since February 2020.

body.h2: Music publishing was trading at pre-pandemic levels but cinemas were not
body.text: For cinemas and theatres, the enforced closure saw trade down to just 10% of pre-pandemic levels, with many closing altogether.

body.h2: Music publishing was trading at pre-pandemic levels but cinemas were not
body.text: By September 2020, with cinemas allowed to reopen with social distancing, turnover was still down 58% on the same month last year.

body.h2: Music publishing was trading at pre-pandemic levels but cinemas were not
body.text: That downturn was not shared by music publishing, which saw an increase in turnover relative to February. This may reflect the increasing use of home entertainment.
